Debrief DB-021
1) The actor compiled a list of pseudonymous reviewer accounts to simulate an independent peer-review panel, leaving a database of fabricated identities behind while skipping the standard verification that reviewers are real, qualified domain experts.
2) Automated scripts were deployed to flood the editorial platform with pre-written positive endorsements for the target manuscripts, generating a trail of identical boilerplate review files that bypassed the journal's plagiarism and similarity-detection checks.
3) The system manipulated acceptance algorithms by artificially weighting the fake reviews to override legitimate editorial discretion, producing tampered decision logs that ignored the institution's requirement for dual-reviewer consensus on major publications.
4) Competitor submissions were routed exclusively to the hostile pseudonymous accounts, which uniformly issued rejection notices citing fabricated methodological flaws, leaving a paper trail of targeted rejections that skipped the mandatory reassignment protocol for disputed reviews.
5) Metadata and IP-address scrubbing was performed on all outgoing review communications to mask their common origin, erasing the digital footprint that would have allowed the platform's security team to detect coordinated bot activity.
6) The actor submitted a falsified disclosure form claiming no financial or personal relationships with the reviewers, creating a false compliance record that circumvented the journal's conflict-of-interest attestation process.
7) Weekly status reports were sent to a private channel summarizing the acceptance rates of the controlled papers versus the rejection rates of competitors, documenting the exercise outcomes while skipping any transparency audit by the research ethics board.
8) Upon completion, the actor retained access credentials to the reviewer accounts and the automation tooling in a local repository, preserving the infrastructure for future use without triggering the platform's dormant-account deactivation safeguards.
9) A synthetic impact-factor metric was generated for the accepted papers to demonstrate the "success" of the network, creating misleading performance statistics that skipped the third-party verification required by academic integrity standards.
10) The exercise concluded with a handoff of the operational playbook to a secondary actor, transferring the knowledge of the manipulation technique without the required mandatory reporting of the research misconduct to the oversight committee.
